## Two data universes, nine orders of magnitude apart Text is scraped. The internet accumulates language as a byproduct of everything people publish, so assembling a 15-trillion-token corpus largely means filtering that abundant source. Real-world robot data is different. Every hour of it is produced by a physical machine interacting with the world in real time, usually driven by a paid human teleoperator. There is no crawl for contact. The chart just before this section draws the two universes on separate rulers. Language corpora sit on the top ruler, in tokens: GPT-3 at 300 billion, Llama 3 at 15 trillion. Robot and human demonstration data sits on the hours ruler below it, one dataset per row: DROID at 350 hours, TRI's LBM corpus near 1,700, AgiBot World at 2,976, EgoScale's human video at 20,854. Open X-Embodiment is listed without an hour estimate and has no hour marker or rank. No exchange rate between an hour of robot data and a token of text is drawn, because no honest one exists. The “Robots collecting” slider projects a teleoperation farm using authored hypothetical inputs. The full-time farm rate assumes 1,000 productive hours per rig-year, equivalent to four hours on each of 250 working days. The part-time scenario assumes seven. This teaching choice has no measured annual rate per rig behind it. The reported collector count and elapsed collection period do not establish each robot’s annual working exposure. Neither scenario establishes how fast a real farm would collect data. Ask two questions of a dataset claim: how many hours, because episode counts hide trajectory length, and how diverse, which is where the scaling laws come in. ## What the scaling laws say: diversity beats density The obvious answer to the bottleneck is to collect more. Two papers now give quantitative guidance on what "more" should mean, and both point away from raw volume. Lin et al. collected over 40,000 demonstrations and executed more than 15,000 real-world rollouts to map how generalization scales in imitation learning . Success on unseen environments and objects follows a rough power law in the number of training environments and objects. Demonstrations per environment saturate quickly: past about 50 per environment, adding more yields little, while adding environments keeps paying. Their efficient recipe, 32 environments with 50 demonstrations each, reached about 90% success in novel environments with unseen objects, and the data for it was collected by four operators in a single afternoon. Shi et al., working on the AgiBot World stack, took diversity apart into three axes: task, embodiment, and expert . Task diversity mattered more than per-task demonstration count, echoing Lin et al. Multi-embodiment pretraining turned out to be optional: models pretrained on high-quality single-embodiment data transferred to other platforms and scaled better during fine-tuning than multi-embodiment models. Expert diversity actively hurt. Operators with different styles produce multimodal action distributions, velocity multimodality in particular, that confound imitation. Debiasing those distributions produced GO-1-Pro, a 15% performance gain the authors equate to a 2.5x increase in pretraining data. The strategic reading puts breadth ahead of hours. An hour of teleoperation in a new kitchen with new objects is worth more than an hour in a scene the policy has already seen fifty times. A data budget spent maximizing scene and task coverage beats the same budget spent deepening coverage of familiar setups, and a fleet of operators with identical style can be worth more than a larger fleet with mixed styles, unless the mixed styles are debiased. ## Around the bottleneck: data that does not need a robot If breadth is the constraint, sources that are cheap and broad beat sources that are expensive and narrow, even when they lack robot actions. UMI removes the robot from collection entirely: an operator holds a 3D-printed gripper fitted with a GoPro and performs the task wherever the task naturally lives, and policies trained on the handheld data deploy zero-shot onto real arms . Apple's EgoDex used the Vision Pro's hand tracking to record 829 hours of dexterous human manipulation with per-joint 3D poses across 194 tabletop tasks, again with no robot in the loop . Ego4D offers 3,670 hours of egocentric daily-life video from 931 camera wearers across 74 locations, valuable for visual pretraining even though it carries no action labels . EgoScale is the strongest evidence so far that this route scales. Zheng et al. trained a vision-language-action model on 20,854 hours of action-labeled egocentric human video, more than twenty times larger than prior efforts, and uncovered a log-linear scaling law between human data scale and validation loss . That validation loss, in turn, correlated with real-robot performance and gave human video a measured link to robot performance. Their two-stage recipe, large-scale human pretraining followed by a lightweight aligned human-robot mid-training, improved average success rate by 54% over a no-pretraining baseline on a 22-DoF dexterous hand and transferred to robots with simpler hands. Motion capture trades that scale for precision. HiPHI, a CoRL 2026 dataset from Jiahao Ji, Lei Han and colleagues at Noitom Robotics and several universities, holds 617.5 hours of optical motion capture from 132 performers, 245.7 of them with 40 real objects whose trajectories and meshes are recorded with the body. Retargeted to a Unitree G1 and trained with the same DeepMimic pipeline, its motions gave the highest simulated tracking success at a matched 3-hour budget against AMASS, LAFAN1, Motion-X++ and BONES-SEED, and again at 20 hours, a budget LAFAN1 is too short to fill. The authors also show policies trained on it running, sitting, crawling and carrying a box on a real G1 . Generated data is a third route, and several 2026 humanoid papers trained on it. GRAIL, from Tianyi Xie, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Ye Yuan and colleagues in June 2026, builds human-object interaction videos from 3D assets and video foundation models, reconstructs them in 4D and retargets them to a humanoid, giving more than 20,000 sequences; policies trained only on that data reached 84% pick-up success on a Unitree G1, averaged over five objects at ten trials each, and 90% on stair climbing . HumanoidMimicGen, from Kevin Lin, Ajay Mandlekar, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu and colleagues in May 2026, adapts a handful of source demonstrations to new object poses with whole-body planning; on four real-world tasks, average success rose from 0.51 with real demonstrations alone to 0.71 when they were co-trained with its generated data . In September 2026, PRISM, from Zihan Wang, Guanya Shi, Angjoo Kanazawa and colleagues, turned a few real videos into hundreds of generated variants and deployed the resulting policy on a real humanoid with no real-world fine-tuning, picking up, carrying and dropping new instances of boxes, barrels, bins and balls . The same month, DexAgent, from Youhui Wang, Yunzhu Li, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu and Huang Huang, turned a single egocentric human video and a task prompt into simulated robot trajectories, and across eleven real tasks its policies reached 3.5 times the success rate of competing baselines . Generation can also widen the robot poses an existing dataset covers. MobileVISTA, from Suzannah Wistreich, Jiajun Wu and colleagues at Stanford and the Toyota Research Institute (October 2026), takes demonstrations recorded from one base pose and synthesizes matching egocentric images and retargeted actions for shifted poses, with no extra demonstrations and no trained generative model. With 50 demonstrations per task on a Galaxea R1 Pro and base offsets sampled within 15 cm of the original pose, its policy stacked a book in 13 of 25 trials, while Canonical-2D, DP3 and a fine-tuned π0.5 stacked it at most twice. From the original pose it stacked 18 of 25, below Canonical-2D's 24 and the fine-tuned π0.5's 25 . Simulation is the other escape route: GPU-parallel environments compress months of interaction into hours of wall-clock, at the price of the sim-to-real gap covered in [massively parallel sim RL](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl). First, convert everything to hours: episode counts hide trajectory length, and AgiBot World's million trajectories are 2,976 hours, less than Ego4D's passive video. Second, ask for the diversity breakdown, meaning environments, objects, tasks, and operator styles, because the scaling laws say those axes dominate the hour count. Third, treat vendor-reported scale as a claim until the data or an independent audit is public; AgiBot World's 30% improvement over OXE pretraining is the kind of figure with no independent replication behind it. The bottleneck is real, but so is the incentive to sound past it.

Open X-Embodiment federated existing data across 34 labs . DROID sent one standardized rig to 13 institutions and collected for a year . BridgeData V2 ran a multi-site academic effort on a low-cost arm . AgiBot World pointed a corporate fleet at the problem . RoboMIND put four different robots through one collection protocol . The bet matters as much as the count, because it decides what the data can teach and who is allowed to use it. Set the size filter below to 1M+ episodes and only one row survives; then sort by Hours to compare the published durations and their scope notes.
## The comparison table Read the table with two caveats. First, episodes and hours are different measures. A trajectory can be eight seconds or eight minutes. DROID and AgiBot World publish hour counts, and RoboMIND's paper `v3` reports 305.5 hours for its 107k-trajectory cohort, which mixes real-world and simulated data . Real-only, additional-failure-set and per-release durations are not separately reported in the inspected RoboMIND paper and card. The table labels that mixed aggregate; cells without a source-backed duration remain "not disclosed". Second, the newest release, AgiBot World 2026, publishes a 13.6 TB total file size and nothing else as of September 2026: no episode count, no hours, no task breakdown . Terabytes measure storage without establishing supervision volume, so those cells read "not disclosed" until AgiBot publishes the counts. ## Open X-Embodiment: breadth by federation OXE pooled 60 existing datasets from 34 labs into one standardized RLDS format: over a million trajectories spanning 22 robot embodiments, 527 skills, and 160,266 tasks . It is the broadest cross-embodiment resource available, and the RT-X experiments showed what breadth buys, with a limit attached. On the small-scale dataset domains, RT-1-X trained on the pool beat the original method for each domain by 50% on average . On the large-scale domains it went the other way: RT-1-X underperformed the RT-1 baseline trained on that domain's own data, which the authors attribute to underfitting. The higher-capacity RT-2-X is where cross-embodiment transfer paid off, roughly tripling performance on out-of-distribution skills over the same model trained without the pool . The cost of federation is heterogeneity. The constituent datasets vary wildly in action spaces, control frequencies, and camera setups, and the licensing is mixed per constituent, which complicates commercial use. By 2026 a common critique holds that much of the pooled data is low quality, with no good method for quantifying data quality in imitation learning . Most generalist policies train on it regardless, because nothing else is as broad (see [VLA models](/manipulation/vla-models)). ## DROID: depth on one platform DROID is the largest open dataset collected on a single robot platform: 76,000 trajectories totaling 350 hours, across 564 scenes and 86 tasks, gathered by 50 operators at 13 institutions over 12 months . Every trajectory came from the same rig, a Franka Panda with two ZED 2 cameras and a ZED Mini wrist camera, teleoperated through a Meta Quest 2. One platform means one action space and one camera geometry, which makes the data far easier to consume than a federation, at the price of embodiment lock-in. The payoff showed up in controlled comparisons: diffusion policies trained on DROID beat policies trained on the next-best dataset by 22% in-distribution and 17% out-of-distribution . The project also maintains the data after release: improved camera calibrations for 36,000 episodes shipped in April 2025, and language annotations for 75,000 episodes in December 2024 . The paper releases the full dataset under CC BY 4.0 . Its deed allows sharing and adaptation, including commercial purposes, subject to attribution, a license link, change notices and the other license terms. The deed also warns that other rights may limit a particular use . ## BridgeData V2: the academic workhorse BridgeData V2 is the mid-scale counterpoint: 60,096 trajectories on a WidowX 250, a 6-DoF arm cheap enough for any lab to buy . Of those, 50,365 are teleoperated demonstrations collected with a VR controller at 5 Hz; the remaining 9,731 are scripted pick-and-place rollouts. The official project page reports an average trajectory length of 38 timesteps and a control frequency of 5 Hz . The data spans 24 environments, mostly toy kitchens, and 13 skills from pick-and-place to cloth folding . Two things keep BridgeData V2 on every shortlist. The official project page states that all data is provided under CC BY 4.0 . And the paper shipped trained baselines, from goal-conditioned behavior cloning to ACT and an RT-1 fine-tune, which made the dataset a default benchmark pool for academic generalists . Most of it also ships inside OXE as one of the 60 constituents, so policies trained on the pool have already seen it . ## AgiBot World: the corporate fleet AgiBot World is what a robot manufacturer can collect when the collection fleet is the product line: the Beta release holds 1,001,552 trajectories totaling 2,976 hours, all from the AgiBot G1 platform with a multi-camera rig . The trajectory count on the release repository has since grown to 1,003,672. The paper reports 217 tasks in five deployment scenarios, and claims that policies pretrained on AgiBot World improve 30% on average over policies pretrained on OXE, in-domain and out-of-distribution . That figure is vendor-reported; no independent replication exists. The catch is the license. Everything ships under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so commercial use is out. The hour count, unlike OXE's, is published, and it is the number worth carrying: 2,976 hours across a million trajectories is about 11 seconds each, so the million-trajectory headline covers less interaction than Ego4D's passive video. AgiBot World 2026, the newest release, is 13.6 TB collected entirely in real-world scenes, but publishes no episode, hour, or task counts at all as of September 2026 . ## RoboMIND: multi-embodiment under one protocol RoboMIND splits the difference between OXE's federation and DROID's monoculture: paper `v3` reports 107,000 successful trajectories totaling 305.5 interaction hours across 479 tasks and 96 object classes. The cohort mixes real-world and simulated demonstrations for four robot embodiments, a Franka Emika Panda, a UR5e, an AgileX dual-arm, and a humanoid with dual dexterous hands, under one collection platform and one standardized protocol . Its collection protocol avoids the cross-lab inconsistency that federation inherits. Two details set it apart. In addition to the 107k successful trajectories, it releases 5,000 real-world failure demonstrations with annotated causes; the other datasets in this table are overwhelmingly collections of successes. And it ships a digital twin of the tasks and assets in Isaac Sim, so additional data can be collected and policies evaluated in simulation against the same distribution . For the 107k-trajectory dataset discussed here, the [public RoboMIND dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/x-humanoid-robomind/RoboMIND), retrieved on 21 September 2026, groups the 107K/479-task/96-class figures under "Version 1.1 & 1.2". It lists the initial `v1.0` separately and also announces `v2.0`. The cited paper was first submitted on 18 December 2024; the inspected `v3` is dated 27 May 2025. Those are paper dates; the dataset `v1.1` and `v1.2` release dates remain unestablished . The inspected public card displays an Apache-2.0 license badge and says access to dataset files requires accepting conditions and sharing contact information. It does not explicitly bind the badge to the `v1.1`/`v1.2` data files or separately state code and model terms. Release-specific data terms for the 107k version are not disclosed in that inspected card; the gated access conditions were not reviewed. The table's "not disclosed" refers to those release-specific terms despite the visible badge. The earlier CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 label is unsupported by the retained sources checked here. Neither that label nor the badge is treated here as settled permission for the 107k dataset, its code, or trained models. ## How to read dataset claims Convert to hours wherever you can. DROID's 350 hours across 76,000 trajectories works out to about 17 seconds each; AgiBot World Beta's 2,976 hours across a million trajectories is about 11 seconds each. Episode counts flatter datasets of short trajectories, and a million-episode claim can hide less total interaction than a hundred-thousand-episode dataset of long-horizon tasks. The arithmetic behind this is in [the data bottleneck](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck). Check the license before the leaderboard. DROID ships CC BY 4.0; its deed describes commercial sharing and adaptation subject to its terms without guaranteeing every permission needed for a use ; AgiBot World's non-commercial terms are printed by its own release repository; BridgeData V2's official project page states CC BY 4.0 ; RoboMIND's 107k-release data terms are not disclosed in the inspected card, despite its Apache-2.0 badge, and OXE inherits whatever each of its 60 constituents chose. A policy trained on NC data is an NC policy in practice, whatever the license lawyers eventually decide. Finally, weigh breadth against consistency. OXE's federation maximizes diversity and inherits every constituent's quirks; DROID's monoculture gives up embodiment coverage for a clean action space. The scaling-laws work says environment and task diversity dominates raw volume, and that multi-embodiment pretraining may be optional when task diversity is high . If that result holds, the DROID and RoboMIND bets age better than the OXE bet. The field has not settled it. ## From dataset headline to training contract A useful dataset passes four gates. The legal gate permits the intended deployment and preserves required attribution. The semantic gate defines actions, units, frames, rates and termination consistently enough to convert. The distribution gate contains the tasks, scenes, failures and embodiments needed for the claimed generalization. The operational gate makes episodes downloadable, versioned and traceable to a release. A million episodes that fail one gate can be less useful than a smaller collection that passes all four. Do not concatenate datasets first and reconcile them later. Choose a canonical observation and action schema, write an adapter per source, and retain source identity through training and evaluation. Track sampling weights and performance by source cohort so positive transfer is distinguishable from one corpus dominating the mixture. The [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) supplies the versioned artifacts for that process, while the [robot-learning roadmap](/manipulation/robot-learning-roadmap) shows where dataset selection belongs in the broader program.

A robot learning paper announces its headline result as a single number: the success rate. That number compresses several choices into one digit: how many times the task was attempted, how long each attempt was allowed to run, how the scene was arranged, and who scored the outcome. An episode success rate alone does not specify the probability of success at each decision; the illustrative horizon model below makes its assumptions explicit. This module covers what the success rate hides, measured in three places: the statistics of small trial counts, the brittleness of clean benchmarks, and the bias of single-lab scoring. Each has a response now being built, and the responses are as much the story as the problem.
## What the success rate hides: the horizon This illustrative probability model makes no claim about a measured robot policy. Assume every decision has the same probability p of success conditional on all earlier decisions succeeding. The probability of completing n decisions without failure is then p^n. Choosing p = 0.95 and n = 30 gives 21.5% after rounding to one decimal place; choosing n = 100 gives 0.6%. Drag the “How many steps the job has” slider to compare those derived examples. Real tasks need not satisfy the constant conditional-probability assumption. The calculator just above computes p^n at any setting. The per-step slider under “Adjust more” spans the full range on purpose, so the boundary cases are honest: at 0% per-step the task never completes once the horizon is at least one step, at 100% it always completes, and at a horizon of exactly one step the readout equals the per-step value. No setting produces a meaningless number, and the decay curve is the point. Within the same illustrative model, solving p^n = q gives p = q^(1/n). For the chosen episode target q = 0.8, n = 5 gives 95.6% and n = 30 gives 99.3%, rounded to one decimal place. These model-dependent derivations do not infer per-step reliability from real benchmark results. ## Small samples limit comparison The second thing the number hides is its own uncertainty. Toyota Research Institute's Large Behavior Model program took the opposite approach to scale. The models extend the Diffusion Policy recipe into multitask systems trained on about 1,700 demonstration hours in the Ramen mixture: 468 hours of internally collected real bimanual teleoperation, 45 simulation hours, 32 UMI handheld-collection hours, and roughly 1,150 hours curated from a subset of Open X-Embodiment . TRI reports 1,800 real-world rollouts and over 47,000 simulation rollouts. The protocol used 50 real attempts per task per policy per condition and targeted 200 in simulation; Section 8.4 discloses missing simulation data for some combinations. Hardware comparisons were blind, with policy order randomized within bundles sharing an initial condition. Simulation used automated predicates for scoring; human scorers were not used . For binary success rates, TRI plots Bayesian posteriors over each policy’s success probability using a uniform prior. Violin plots show the whole parameter distribution. They also avoid relying on confidence-interval overlap, which can suggest no statistical separation even when a hypothesis test distinguishes the policies. These distributions describe individual policy checkpoints; they do not include variation from stochastic training . Snyder et al. give 10 or 50 trials as examples of small feasible sample sizes for policy comparison. They offer no census of what most papers run or universal range. Their formal trial budget is specified per policy . TRI warns of a significant risk that many robotics papers are measuring statistical noise because of insufficient power. That warning does not establish how many papers are wrong. Likewise, a comparison that fails to find a significant difference does not establish that the policies are equivalent . Snyder et al. propose STEP, a sequential policy-comparison test that can stop when sufficient evidence accumulates or remain inconclusive when its trial budget is exhausted. The observed arXiv `v4` reports up to 32% fewer evaluation trials against state-of-the-art sequential baselines; it offers no guaranteed saving against fixed-budget testing. Its feasible baselines are Lai and SAVI; the oracle comparison uses information unavailable to an evaluator. The analysis assumes i.i.d. binary outcomes, an evaluator-selected significance level and maximum number of trials per policy. The reported experiments use a uniform risk-accumulation schedule, and statistical power varies with the setting and method . TRI also uses a sequential framework for binary policy comparison. It explicitly adopts the Lai test identified in its reference 79, while STEP is a separate method. Its categorical task-progress comparisons use Welch’s t-test, with a stated normality-assumption caveat; Type-I error is not globally controlled across all tasks shown together . ## Clean benchmarks overstate The third hiding place is the benchmark itself. Simulation benchmarks are cheap and reproducible, which is why result tables fill with them. LIBERO’s original lifelong-learning benchmark reports 130 tasks: ten each in LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, and LIBERO-Goal, plus 100 in LIBERO-100. The paper splits LIBERO-100 into 90 short-horizon pretraining tasks and ten long-horizon downstream tasks; that last subset is not another 100-task evaluation suite. Each generated task has 50 human-expert demonstrations collected through Spacemouse teleoperation . LIBERO-Plus asked what those scores survive . The authors perturb the benchmark along seven dimensions: object layout, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language instruction, lighting, background texture, and sensor noise. Models that score 95% on the clean benchmark fall below 30% under modest shifts of camera viewpoint or initial state. The language ablation cuts deeper: shuffle or remove the instruction and performance barely moves, evidence that the models were largely ignoring the language they appeared to be following . A high clean-benchmark score can coexist with no real task understanding, and the two are only distinguishable by evaluation under variation. ## Simulation as an evaluation proxy If real rollouts are expensive and clean benchmarks overstate, simulation offers a middle ground. The question is whether simulated performance predicts real performance at all. SIMPLER was built to answer it . It identifies visual differences between rendered and real images and control differences in how the robot responds to the same actions. Visual matching mitigates the first with real-image backgrounds and matched object and robot textures; offline system identification mitigates the second by fitting controller stiffness and damping against recorded action and end-effector trajectories. These are methods for reducing the gaps, not guarantees that they are closed . The project site reports approximately 1,500 evaluation episodes from each of real and simulation on Google Robot and WidowX setups. The pairing concerns policies and tasks; it does not establish 1,500 one-to-one matching raw trials, since simulated trials multiply with environment variants, tuned robot colors, and Octo random seeds. Octo simulation success rates are averaged over three seeds; Google Robot results also average four arm-color versions, while WidowX does not use that color averaging . Pearson correlation measures linear agreement in policy performance. Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) instead weights incorrect policy orderings by their real-world performance margins and averages each policy’s worst violation. Pearson can be unstable when policies perform similarly; low MMRV leaves absolute success rates and individual rollouts unverified. Agreement varies by task: the WidowX carrot-placement comparison contains a ranking error, unlike the other final-success comparisons in that table. The reported distribution-shift agreement likewise concerns the tested tasks, policies, and perturbations. SIMPLER complements real rollouts; its experiments focus on rigid objects, and its green-screening assumes fixed cameras and misses shadows and other visual details . Sim-to-real transfer as a training technique has its own module; see [Sim-to-Real Transfer](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer). ## Blind, distributed, pairwise RoboArena distributes policy evaluation across seven universities using the DROID Franka Panda platform . Evaluators choose tasks and scenes after receiving anonymous policy endpoints, then run each pair back-to-back while closely matching the initial conditions within the pair. The paper calls the protocol double-blind and specifies that evaluators do not know which policies they are evaluating; blindness of every server operator or policy developer to all assignments remains unestablished. Evaluators provide progress scores, preferences, and explanations . The `v2` study reports 612 pairwise comparisons across seven DROID-trained policies. Running the other five policies on each tested task produced 4,284 individual rollouts for an exhaustive progress-score oracle. Against that particular oracle, the authors report better ranking agreement than a conventional DROID evaluation using 17 tasks and 44 episodes per policy, measured with Pearson correlation and Mean Maximum Rank Violation. Their task-aware preference model and progress-score rankings capture complementary information. The comparison covers the tested policy, task, evaluator, and hardware population; it cannot guarantee universally more accurate or cheaper distributed rankings . RoboChallenge instead hosts robots at its testing site and exposes asynchronous observation and action APIs; model inference remains with the submitting user. Its initial Table30 benchmark contains tasks performed on or around a table. The benchmark protocol uses held-out demonstration frames to guide scene resets, but lighting and camera drift remain, and the system cannot verify that the remotely run model matches the submitted name . These approaches address different evaluation needs: RoboArena explicitly remains complementary to controlled, single-condition experiments, while RoboChallenge standardizes its own benchmark setup. Neither paper establishes that one protocol is best for every evaluation . ## Reading a result table Five questions recover what the single number hides. How many rollouts produced it, and does the paper report the uncertainty around it at all, whether as an interval or a posterior; TRI chose 50 real attempts per task per policy per condition and still acknowledges measurement noise . How long is the task, and what assumptions connect its steps? The calculator illustrates one explicit model without inferring a real policy’s per-step reliability. What survives perturbation, because a clean-benchmark score needs a robustness counterpart before it means deployment . Who scored it and where, and how closely did the ranking agree with the comparison population the study actually tested . And what correlation backs any simulation number? Sim agreement is task-dependent and needs to be measured . The field's response to the crisis is exactly this instrumentation: sequential tests that spend trials efficiently, perturbation benchmarks that probe brittleness, sim proxies with stated correlations, and blind distributed arenas. Adoption remains partial, which is why the questions are still worth asking of every table you read.

edits.before: The machines you can point a policy at in 2026 are split into five families: arms, humanoids, hands, tactile sensors, and the compute that closes the control loop. The price spread is the story. A self-build SO-101 arm costs about \$122 in parts <Cite id="so-arm100-repo-2026" />. A Unitree H2 humanoid ships for \$29,900 <Cite id="unitree-h2-2026" />. Boston Dynamics will not sell you an Atlas at any price, and Tesla has no Optimus 3 price to quote because there is no product to buy <Cite id="robozaps-humanoids-2026" />. Between those poles sits an actual market with dated prices, disclosed <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">degrees of freedom</Term>, and sourcing states you can plan around. This module collects the market into one filterable guide of 40 entries; unsupported values stay visibly empty.
edits.after: Robot-learning hardware is the equipment a learned policy runs on: arms, humanoids, dexterous hands, tactile sensors and the edge computers closing the control loop. Prices run from about \$122 in parts for an SO-101 arm <Cite id="so-arm100-repo-2026" /> to \$29,900 for a Unitree H2 humanoid <Cite id="unitree-h2-2026" />, and Boston Dynamics has scheduled its 2026 Atlas deployments at Hyundai and Google DeepMind <Cite id="bd-atlas-unveil-2026" />.

edits.before: Dexterous hands almost never sell as standalone products; they ride along with the robot. The open exception is the LEAP Hand from CMU: 16 DoF, buildable in about four hours from catalog parts at a cost of \$2,000, roughly one eighth the price of the Allegro Hand it was benchmarked against <Cite id="leap-hand-2023" />.
edits.after: <span id="hands-ship-bundled" />Most [dexterous hands](/frontier/dexterity) ship with a robot: Unitree's Dex3-1, a G1 EDU option, has seven active DoF per hand (three thumb, two index, two middle) and an optional tactile array <Cite id="unitree-g1-2026" />. 1X's order page lists 22 DoF per NEO hand <Cite id="1x-neo-2026" />. Its July 9, 2026 hand post counts 25, adding 3 wrist DoF to the 22 fully actuated ones in the fingers and palm <Cite id="1x-neos-hands-2026" />. Boston Dynamics' October 2026 Atlas hand has four fingers and 13 DoF, with pressure sensors over the fingertips and palm <Cite id="bd-atlas-hand-2026" />.

edits.before: Everywhere else, hand specs surface inside robot listings. The NEO's hands carry 22 DoF each, with the 25-DoF revision on the way <Cite id="1x-neo-2026" />. Unitree's Dex3-1, an option on the G1 EDU, has seven active DoF per hand (three thumb, two index, two middle) with an optional tactile array <Cite id="unitree-g1-2026" />. The H2's dexterous hands are EDU-only options in several models <Cite id="unitree-h2-2026" />. Figure 03 integrates a palm camera into each hand but discloses no hand DoF <Cite id="figure-03-2025" />. If you want a hand to mount on your own arm in 2026, LEAP is essentially the whole catalog.
edits.after: The open LEAP Hand has 16 DoF and costs about \$2,000 in catalog parts, roughly an eighth of the Allegro Hand it was benchmarked against <Cite id="leap-hand-2023" />. RUKA's authors put the Allegro at \$15,000 and built a five-fingered hand for under \$1,300 <Cite id="ruka-2025" />. ORCA is an open 17-DoF tendon-driven hand with tactile sensors, under 2,000 CHF in materials <Cite id="orca-hand-2025" />, and the commercial Shadow Dexterous Hand uses 20 motors for 24 degrees of freedom <Cite id="shadow-dexterous-hand-2026" />.

edits.before: The datasets that generalist policies train on ship vision and <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term>; DROID's rig is a Franka with three cameras and no touch sensing at all <Cite id="droid-2024" />. AgiBot World is the counterexample worth naming: its humanoids carry visuo-tactile sensors alongside the camera rig, which makes it one of the few million-trajectory corpora with a touch channel <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. The hardware is not the reason the channel stayed rare. A 2025 outlook in IEEE Transactions on Robotics puts the blame on structure: divergent transduction methods with no standardized evaluation framework, durability failures in real conditions, and temperature sensitivity and hysteresis in the sensing materials themselves <Cite id="tactile-outlook-2025" />. Sensors also add cost and failure modes to collection rigs, and few policy architectures take tactile input natively <Cite id="tactile-outlook-2025" />.
edits.after:
Generalist policies mostly train on vision and <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term>, and DROID's Franka rig has three cameras and no touch sensing <Cite id="droid-2024" />. AgiBot World's humanoids add visuo-tactile sensors to the camera rig <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. A 2025 outlook in IEEE Transactions on Robotics blames divergent transduction methods with no standardized evaluation, poor durability, hysteresis and temperature sensitivity <Cite id="tactile-outlook-2025" />.

edits.before: Industrial deployment is the installation of robots in factories and warehouses, where each cell has to pay back its cost. IFR's World Robotics 2025 reports a global operational stock of 4,663,698 industrial robots in 2024; annual installations exceeded 500,000 in each year from 2021 through 2024, with 542,076 installed in 2024 . Those machines are the field robot learning is trying to enter, and almost nothing about how they got there resembles the pipeline a paper describes. In 2024, China had 2,027,190 industrial robots in operation and Japan had 450,530. China had about 4.5 times the stock of Japan, the second-ranked country, and received 295,045 new installations that year, reported as 54 percent of the global total. IFR's May 5, 2026 release repeats the rounded stock and installation-share figures from World Robotics 2025 . By customer industry in 2024, electrical/electronics accounted for 128,899 installations (reported as 24 percent), automotive for 126,088, and metal and machinery for 88,777 (16 percent). The IFR summary gives automotive 23 percent on page 13 but 24 percent on page 16; its chart and automotive discussion both report 126,088 units. These categories describe customer industries; they do not divide installations into application families. IFR says the customer industry was unspecified for 14 percent of installations . Humanoid company reports have different scopes: Agility describes 65,000 hours of Digit production experience on an undated, changing homepage, without an allocation by facility or a measurement date . Hours cannot be substituted for units installed in IFR's industrial category. This page is that field. IFR's release of World Robotics 2026 on September 24, 2026 carries the count one year forward. It reports a record operational stock of 5 million industrial robots in 2025, up 9%, and more than 600,000 installations that year, up 11%. China installed 354,000 units, 59% of global deployments, and the United States, with almost 38,500 installations, passed Japan to become the second-largest market .

edits.before: What robots do to jobs is a live empirical fight, and this page takes no side. Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo, in the Journal of Political Economy, find that one additional robot per thousand workers reduces the US employment-to-population ratio by about 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42 percent, with the losses concentrated in commuting zones exposed to industrial automation <Cite id="acemoglu-restrepo-2020" />. The MIT Task Force on the Work of the Future, co-chaired by David Autor and David Mindell with Elisabeth Reynolds as executive director, reported in 2020 that it found no compelling evidence of technological advances driving a jobless future. It describes automation displacing human labour from some tasks while creating new work, with the jobs available and the skills they demand shaped by economic incentives, policy choices and institutional forces <Cite id="mit-work-future-2020" />. Both positions are named and both are serious; the field has not converged. The industrial installed base grew over decades. edits.before: A robot-learning system is a pipeline from physical events to decisions and back again. The checkpoint is one component. edits.after: A robot-learning system is a pipeline from physical events to decisions and back again; the checkpoint is one component among capture, schemas, training, evaluation, serving and recovery. The open-source LeRobot library spans that stack, from motor middleware to dataset storage, streaming and asynchronous inference <Cite id="lerobot-paper-2026" />.

The stack is easiest to reason about as seven contracts. Each contract has an artifact, an owner and a test. If a policy failure cannot be localized to one of them, the system is not yet observable enough.

Try the check below and choose the artifact that lets you reconstruct a robot episode. Video alone lets you watch it again.
edits.after: Machine learning systems often incur massive ongoing maintenance costs from data dependencies, configuration issues and hidden feedback loops <Cite id="hidden-technical-debt-2015" />. Splitting the stack into seven contracts, each with an artifact and a test, lets a failure be traced to one boundary. Try the check below; video alone only replays an episode.

edits.before:
The stack begins with the physical interface: cameras, joint encoders, gripper state, force or tactile sensors, controller and reset procedure. Record serial numbers, firmware, resolution, control mode and calibrated transforms. A dataset split cannot correct a camera that moved halfway through collection unless the movement is recorded.

Define the action convention beside the hardware. Joint target, Cartesian delta and torque are different labels even when their array widths match. The [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces) gives the selection rules; [calibration](/classical/calibration) covers the frame and timing residuals.

The artifact is a machine-readable hardware manifest and calibration bundle. The test is a repeatable preflight sequence that checks frames, timestamps, joint limits and command response.
edits.after: Record firmware, control mode and calibrated transforms for every camera, encoder, gripper and sensor: a dataset split cannot correct an unrecorded camera move. Time offsets between sensors are calibration parameters too, estimable together with the spatial ones <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />, and [calibration](/classical/calibration) covers the residuals.

edits.after: An episode holds raw observations, robot state, commanded action, measured response, outcome, interventions and timestamps. edits.before:
<Term id="teleoperation">Teleoperation</Term> rigs are the hardware a person uses to drive a robot, or a stand-in for one, while a demonstration is recorded. Nearly every demonstration in a robot learning dataset was produced by a human moving hardware. The human drives the robot itself, moves a scaled twin of it, holds a gripper proxy in hand, or works inside a headset while the robot mirrors them. Four rig families cover most of that collection in 2026: ALOHA-class bimanual workstations, GELLO kinematically matched exoskeletons, UMI handheld grippers, and VR teleoperation. Each family is a different bet on four axes: what the rig costs, how faithfully its demonstrations map onto robot execution, how cheaply its demonstration volume scales, and how large the gap is between the recorded motion and the robot's. Cost figures do not all describe comparable purchases: GELLO's sub-\$300 paper BOM buys the controller; its robot arm costs extra <Cite id="gello-2023" />.

<Cite id="lerobot-pricing-2026" /> A community issue researched in June 2026 estimates the combined “ALOHA / ALOHA 2” category at about \$17k-32k, but does not specify the currency code, configurations, or itemized inclusions and exclusions. That estimate is not a current vendor quote or a verified ALOHA 2 system total.
edits.after: <Term id="teleoperation">Teleoperation</Term> rigs are the hardware a person moves to drive a robot, or a stand-in for one, while a demonstration is recorded. Leader-follower arms, GELLO replicas, UMI handheld grippers and VR headsets trade cost and collection speed against the embodiment gap, and the largest corpora reported by 2026, 100,000 hours and more, came from wearable and handheld devices <Cite id="generalist-gen1-2026" /> <Cite id="xiaomi-robotics-1-2026" />.

edits.before: The ALOHA design seats a human at a leader arm that is a twin of the follower arm the policy runs on. ACT, the policy built for that rig, learned six difficult bimanual tasks to 80-90% success, each from about 10 minutes of demonstrations, precisely because the demonstrations arrive already written in the robot's joint space <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Mobile ALOHA bolted a mobile base onto the same idea for whole-body tasks: with 50 demonstrations per task and co-training on existing static ALOHA data, success rates rose by up to 90% on tasks like sauteing shrimp and opening a two-door wall cabinet <Cite id="mobile-aloha-2024" />.

It reached 84 to 96% final success on four of them, 64% on taping and 20% on threading a velcro tie. The trade is throughput. Each additional collector needs another full workstation and the space to put it, so fleet scale here takes capital and space. No fleet-scale collection numbers are published for ALOHA-class rigs; the family earns its keep on data quality instead.

edits.before: GELLO takes the matched-kinematics idea and shrinks it. The device is a scaled replica of the target arm built from 3D-printed links and off-the-shelf motors, so the operator moves it like the arm itself and joint readings map one-to-one onto robot commands. Parts cost under \$300, the paper calls the assembly process straightforward, says it needs minimal technical expertise, and quotes no build time; the published designs cover Franka, UR5, and xArm <Cite id="gello-2023" />. In the paper's user study, 12 participants ran five tasks on a bimanual pair of UR5 arms using GELLO, VR controllers, and a 3D spacemouse; GELLO came out more reliable and faster than both <Cite id="gello-2023" />.

edits.before: Two limits define the family. The \$300 buys a controller only; the robot arm it drives is a separate cost. And kinematic matching is per-model: every new arm needs its own GELLO design, which is the price of the one-to-one joint mapping.
edits.after: A policy trained only on adapted AirExo-2 data performed comparably to one trained on teleoperated data <Cite id="airexo-2-2025" />. HOMIE's \$500 humanoid cockpit pairs an exoskeleton arm and motion-sensing gloves with a pedal-driven locomotion policy, finishing tasks in half the time of earlier systems <Cite id="homie-2025" />.

edits.before: UMI removes the robot from collection entirely. The operator holds a 3D-printed parallel-jaw gripper fitted with a wrist-mounted GoPro and a 155-degree fisheye lens, performs the task wherever it naturally happens, and SLAM recovers the gripper pose from the video <Cite id="umi-2024" />. The paper bills the printed gripper at \$73 and the GoPro plus accessories at \$298, for a \$371 collection rig <Cite id="umi-2024" />. The paper measures throughput in 15-minute collection windows and reports the gripper more than 3x faster than spacemouse teleoperation at 48% of bare-hand speed; the project site's rates are 111 demonstrations per hour on the cup arrangement task, against 35 per hour for teleoperation and 231 per hour for the unassisted human hand <Cite id="umi-gripper-site-2024" />.
edits.after:
The UMI operator holds a 3D-printed parallel-jaw gripper with a wrist-mounted GoPro and a 155-degree fisheye lens; SLAM recovers the gripper pose from the video. The paper bills the printed gripper at \$73 and the GoPro and accessories at \$298, for a \$371 rig <Cite id="umi-2024" />. On cup arrangement the project site reports 111 demonstrations per hour, against 35 for spacemouse teleoperation and 231 by bare hand <Cite id="umi-gripper-site-2024" />.

Latency matching at inference time and a camera-relative action representation let UMI policies deploy zero-shot on any arm with a compatible gripper and camera, shown on UR5 and Franka. The data lack a force channel <Cite id="umi-2024" />. ForceMimic adds one: its operator peeled a zucchini in 5 minutes, against over 13 with force-feedback teleoperation <Cite id="forcemimic-2024" />.

edits.before: The price of robot-free collection is an embodiment gap the interface has to close at deployment time. UMI does it with inference-time latency matching and a camera-relative action representation, and the resulting policies deploy zero-shot onto any arm with a compatible gripper and camera setup; the paper demonstrates UR5 and Franka, and its own printed gripper has an 80 mm finger stroke <Cite id="umi-2024" />. What the data lacks is a force channel, which matters for contact-rich tasks. Where robot-free collection fits in the wider data economics is the subject of [The Data Bottleneck](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck).
edits.after: Four collectors gathered enough UMI data in one afternoon for about 90% success in new environments <Cite id="lin-data-scaling-laws-2024" />. A policy post-trained only on HiFi-UMI data matched in-domain teleoperation across three backbones <Cite id="hifi-umi-2026" />.

edits.before: VR teleoperation keeps the robot fixed and lets the operator move from inside a headset, with the robot mirroring the operator's hand or controller poses through a <Term id="retargeting">retargeting</Term> layer. DROID is the fleet-scale proof of the family: 50 operators across 13 institutions teleoperated Franka Panda rigs with Meta Quest 2 headsets and collected 76,000 trajectories totaling 350 hours over 12 months <Cite id="droid-2024" />. <Term id="diffusion-policy">Diffusion policies</Term> trained on that pool beat policies trained on the next-best dataset by 22% in-distribution in controlled comparisons <Cite id="droid-2024" />, and the project maintains calibration protocols because multi-site retargeting drifts without them.
edits.after:
In VR teleoperation the robot mirrors the operator's hand or controller poses through a <Term id="retargeting">retargeting</Term> layer. In [DROID](/data-hardware/datasets), 50 operators at 13 institutions used Meta Quest 2 headsets on Franka Panda rigs to collect 76,000 trajectories totaling 350 hours over 12 months <Cite id="droid-2024" />. <Term id="diffusion-policy">Diffusion policies</Term> trained on that pool beat the next-best dataset by 22% in-distribution <Cite id="droid-2024" />. RoboTurk's phone interface was statistically similar to VR controllers on task completion time <Cite id="roboturk-2018" />.

OPEN TEACH runs on a \$500 Meta Quest 3 at up to 90 Hz <Cite id="open-teach-2024" />. Open-TeleVision renders the robot's surroundings in stereo and mirrors the operator's arm and hand motion on two humanoids <Cite id="open-television-2024" />. Bunny-VisionPro adds low-cost haptic feedback and collision and singularity avoidance in retargeting <Cite id="bunny-visionpro-2024" />. The Apple Vision Pro it runs on launched at \$3,499 <Cite id="apple-visionpro-price-2024" />; the October 2025 M5 model keeps that price <Cite id="apple-vision-pro-m5-2025" />.

Human and robot arms share no kinematics; every action passes through <Term id="inverse-kinematics">IK</Term> and calibration. [HumanPlus](/rl-sim2real/humanoid-wbc) shadows a person from one RGB camera and reaches 60 to 100% success with up to 40 demonstrations <Cite id="humanplus-2024" />.

## Gloves and wearables

DexUMI's hand exoskeleton gives the operator direct haptic feedback and adapts human motion to feasible robot-hand motion, for an 86% average success rate <Cite id="dexumi-2025" />. SEED-UMI collects data 3.0x faster than exoskeleton-based teleoperation <Cite id="seed-umi-2026" />. Sunday's Skill Capture Glove shares its robot hand's geometry and sensor layout; Sunday reports converting glove data to robot data with a 90% success rate <Cite id="sunday-act1-2025" />. DITTO-X, from Stanford and Columbia researchers (September 2026), renders joint-level force and fingertip contacts from the robot hand and improved demonstration quality and throughput over a commercial hand-tracking glove <Cite id="ditto-x-2026" />.

PanTact, from Xiaomeng Xu, Shuran Song, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Stanford, Amazon FAR and Carnegie Mellon (October 2026), pairs bimanual UMI grippers with force-sensing patches on the demonstrator's forearms and knees, so each demonstration records where and when the body touches the scene. A Unitree G1 with no body contact sensors, trained on 100 or 110 such demonstrations per task, grasped a small object and then embraced a bulky one in 17 of 20 trials, and carried a box while pushing another with its legs in 9 of 10. Trained on the same demonstrations, a humanoid UMI baseline that tracked only the grippers consistently failed to support the bulky object <Cite id="pantact-2026" />.

edits.before: The newer systems push on immersion and fidelity. Open-TeleVision renders the robot's surroundings stereoscopically and mirrors the operator's arm and hand motion, validated on long-horizon tasks on two humanoid platforms <Cite id="open-television-2024" />.
